core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Diverticulitis (uncomplicated) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes CT confirmation of disease severity, supportive care with hydration and analgesia, and reserving antibiotics for complicated or higher-risk presentations, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe left lower abdominal pain, fever, and change in bowel habits for 3 days
Key HPI features: 62M presents with 3 days of constant, aching pain in the left lower quadrant of his abdomen, accompanied by a fever of 38.2C, mild nausea, and new onset of constipation.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.2C, HR 92, BP 132/84. Left lower quadrant tenderness to palpation with mild voluntary guarding, no rebound or rigidity. Labs show mild leukocytosis. CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulosis with pericolic fat stranding, consistent with uncomplicated acute diverticulitis, without abscess, free air, or perforation.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Diverticulitis (uncomplicated).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Colorectal cancer without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Diffuse peritonitis (suggests free perforation).
management_principles: Order CT scan of the abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast to confirm uncomplicated disease and exclude abscess or perforation
Provide supportive care with hydration, analgesia, and dietary advancement as tolerated
Reserve antibiotics for complicated disease, systemic illness, immunocompromise, or other higher-risk presentations
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Micro-perforation or inflammation of a colonic diverticulum, classically causing left lower quadrant pain, fever, and a change in bowel habits — the 'left-sided appendicitis'.
red_flags: Inability to tolerate oral intake with high fever

must_ask.objective: Location and character of the pain
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and has it been constant or crampy?
How many days has this been going on?
Has there been any change in your bowel habits, like constipation?
Have you ever been diagnosed with diverticulitis before?

history.answer: I've had severe pain in the lower left side of my belly and a fever for the past three days.
It started gradually about three days ago as a dull ache and has become steadily more severe.
The pain is down in the lower left side of my abdomen, and it has stayed in that exact area without moving.
No, it doesn't spread anywhere else like my back, shoulder, or groin.
It feels like a constant, heavy aching and throbbing pain rather than cramps that come and go.
Right now I would rate it around a seven out of ten, and it has definitely gotten stronger over the last few days.
It has been hurting constantly without letting up for three days straight.
Walking around, coughing, or bumping against things makes it throb more, while curling up still eases it slightly; eating also seems to make it worse.
I've had slight twinges on that side once or twice in recent years, but never anything this painful or lasting.
I have felt mildly sick to my stomach since yesterday, but I haven't actually thrown up.
I've been quite constipated and haven't had a bowel movement in two days, although I am still able to pass gas.
No, I haven't had any diarrhea, and there has been no red blood or dark tarry stool.
Yes, I've been feeling chilly and feverish, and when I took my temperature this morning it was 38.2 degrees.
No, my eyes and skin look their normal color, and my urine hasn't turned dark brown or stools clay-colored.
No burning or pain when I urinate, no blood in my urine, and no need to pee more often than usual.
No, I haven't felt dizzy, lightheaded, or faint at all.
No chest pain, chest tightness, or shortness of breath.
I haven't eaten anything greasy or out of the ordinary, and I haven't had any alcoholic drinks recently.
I tried taking two acetaminophen pills yesterday, but they barely helped, and I haven't taken aspirin or ibuprofen.
I have high blood pressure, but I don't have any irregular heart rhythm like atrial fibrillation or blood vessel blockages.
During a routine colonoscopy about five years ago, the doctor mentioned I had small pouches or diverticula in my colon, but I never had an infection diagnosed.
I'm wondering if one of those colon pouches got infected, or if this could be something more serious like bowel cancer.
I'm really worried that my intestine might tear or burst open and cause a serious abdominal infection.
I was hoping to get a CT scan to see what is going on inside and receive IV antibiotics to clear up the infection.
I have high blood pressure and I've dealt with chronic constipation for many years.
I had my appendix removed when I was a young man in my twenties, but no other surgeries or hospital admissions.
I take Lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day every morning for my blood pressure, and sometimes an over-the-counter fiber supplement.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco.
I might have a single glass of wine on a special occasion, but I haven't had a drink in months.
I am retired and live at home with my wife.
My father had high blood pressure and died of a heart attack in his seventies, and my mother had hypertension, but nobody had colon cancer.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, heart rate 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 38.2 C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Flat abdomen with an old well-healed surgical scar in the right lower quadrant, no distension, erythema, or visible pulsation.
Hypoactive bowel sounds present in all four quadrants with no vascular bruits.
Tympanitic note throughout with localized percussion tenderness over the left lower quadrant.
Marked focal tenderness to palpation in the left lower quadrant with mild voluntary guarding, but no involuntary muscular rigidity.
No rebound tenderness elicited in any abdominal quadrant.
Negative Murphy sign with no tenderness or inspiratory arrest in the right upper quadrant.
No tenderness at McBurney point; psoas sign and obturator sign are negative.
Normal sphincter tone with no palpable rectal masses, no focal rectal wall tenderness, and no gross blood on the examining glove.
